Victory:
  - BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA + DESTROY_OBJECT on KING reaching area (93,56)-(97,60); SCOUT_CAVALRY (player 3) [path "VC"]

  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "Defeat - Emperor Lost"]
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on VILLAGER_MALE (player 1) [path "Defeat - Treasury Lost"]
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KNIGHT (player 2) [path "Defeat - Sultan's Wrath"]
issues_found: SALADIN is placed as the Mamluk court figure, but Saladin died in 1193 and was Ayyubid; the sultan in 1324 was al-Nasir Muhammad. The engine ships no al-Nasir hero, so a renamed generic unit (e.g. a King or Cavalry Archer) was the correct and available choice — placing a hero 130 years out of period is avoidable error.

Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the architecture set of Mali's caravan and of Cairo's citadel is left to chance; Saracens (and, in DE, Malians/Berbers) were available and would have fixed both building sets.

The Mali contingent is represented only by CAMEL_RIDER, a KING, and villagers; nothing distinguishes a West African imperial caravan (no Malian-specific units, no camel/pack-train object beyond a single male villager as 'treasury'), and its market/tents are generically medieval.

The desert-raider ambush (player 3 SCOUT_CAVALRY/ARCHER with a 'Raider Chief') is invented; no source records an attack on Musa's caravan on the approach to Cairo. Victory is partly gated on killing this invented unit.
The protocol crisis is resolved by the court simply being 'awed'; the sources record Musa's own compromise (he prostrated to God, not the sultan), which the text omits.
Only 176 objects on a 120x120 map, with a caravan of ~13 units, badly understates the 'enormous caravan' the narration itself stresses.
The defeat triggers all use DECLARE_VICTORY rather than a loss action (a well-formedness matter, but it also means the 'Sultan's Wrath' outcome does not actually punish the player).
strengths: Correct date and figures named in text: July 1324, Mansa Musa, Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, hajj to Mecca.
The gold-distribution episode and its documented consequence (the price of gold in Egypt depressed for years) is scripted as its own dialogue beat.
The prostration-protocol dispute — the single best-remembered incident of the Cairo visit — is given a dedicated trigger, herald, and dialogue exchange.
Victory is keyed to bringing the KING (Mansa Musa) into the citadel courtyard area rather than to combat, and defeat to losing the emperor or the treasury — the escort/diplomacy shape of the history.
Terrain furnishings (palm forest, rock formations, gold mines, camels, cliffs) read plausibly as a desert route toward the Nile.
justification: The scenario's narrative scaffolding is unusually faithful — the 1324 date, the hajj, the alms-giving that crashed the price of gold, and the prostration crisis at al-Nasir Muhammad's court are all present and correctly ordered, and victory is properly keyed to escorting the KING (Musa) into the citadel rather than to slaughter. It is undermined by casting SALADIN, dead since 1193, as the Mamluk court's figurehead when a renamed generic unit was available, and by leaving both civilizations RANDOM so that neither Mali's caravan nor Cairo's citadel has a determined architecture. The invented desert-raider ambush, whose chief must be killed as part of the victory condition, adds a combat episode the sources do not support, and the tiny 13-unit 'enormous caravan' contradicts the scenario's own narration.

Smaller lapses include camel riders and mangonels in a steppe cavalry force, a cavalry-heavy Russian centre where infantry militia stood, and the closing claim that Mamai died on the field when he in fact fled and was killed later in Crimea.

Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture, unit skins and bonuses are unassigned - the Byzantine keep/monastery and the Seljuk camp may render as anything from Japanese to Mesoamerican.

TREE_PALM_FOREST x8 on the map: Manzikert lies on the high, semi-arid Armenian plateau near Lake Van, not a palm environment. The 'desert riders' line in Romanos' dialogue compounds this misplacement.
Romanos' dialogue calls his troops 'legions' and claims a three-to-one advantage; Byzantine superiority at Manzikert was real but nowhere near that ratio, and the term is five centuries out of date.

The 'Byzantine Reserve Committed' trigger sends reinforcements forward, inverting the actual event: Andronikos Doukas withdrew the reserve from the field, a treachery at least as decisive as the mercenary desertion.

CROSSBOWMAN for Byzantine missile troops in 1071 is an engine-imposed approximation, but the absence of any representation of the Varangian/Frankish (Roussel de Bailleul) or Armenian contingents leaves the Byzantine roster generic.
Objectives text speaks of 'cataphract captains' while the Byzantine roster contains Cavaliers and Champions with no distinguished cataphract unit.

The mercenary defection is modelled mechanically via CHANGE_OWNERSHIP after Byzantine losses, reproducing the desertion of Romanos' mercenary wing.
A 'Feigned Retreat - Ambush Sprung' trigger keyed to BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA with unit creation reproduces the classic Turkic feigned withdrawal and encirclement used at Manzikert.

Victory fires on the death/capture of the Byzantine KING representing Romanos IV, matching the historical outcome, and defeat on the loss of the Seljuk commander or the overrunning of the Sultan's camp.
Narration correctly states the date (August 1071), place (Manzikert, eastern Anatolia), both commanders by name, and the consequence: Romanos captured and Anatolia opened to the Seljuks.
Tents, pavilions and a bonfire-lit Seljuk camp opposite a Byzantine keep give a legible field-army-versus-field-army layout rather than a siege.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of Manzikert right - horse archers wearing down a heavier Byzantine line, a feigned retreat and encirclement, the mercenary wing changing sides, and victory keyed specifically to the capture of the emperor with defeat on the sultan's fall or the camp being overrun. It is undermined by casting SALADIN, a 12th-century Ayyubid, as Alp Arslan when a renamed generic cavalry unit was available, by leaving both civilizations RANDOM so no Byzantine or Turkish architecture is guaranteed, and by palm forest on the Armenian plateau. The invented 'reserve committed' event also reverses Andronikos Doukas' actual withdrawal, and the 'legions'/'three to one' dialogue is loose, though a playthrough would still leave the player with the correct commanders, date, tactics and outcome.

Narration correctly dates the event to January 1258, names Caliph Al-Musta'sim, and gives the roughly two-week duration of the siege before the sack.
